chief_complaint: sudden chest tightness, wheezing, and coughing while exercising in cold air
hpi_details: 2-year history of reproducible, predictable episodes of acute shortness of breath, chest tightness, audible wheezing, and dry coughing that occur almost exclusively 5 to 10 minutes after initiating high-intensity aerobic exercise (especially running outdoor football matches or cycling in cold winter air). Symptoms peak 5 to 10 minutes after stopping exercise and resolve spontaneously within 30 to 45 minutes of rest. Denies waking up at night with coughing, denies shortness of breath during rest at home, and denies seasonal hay fever. Can sit in a classroom or work at his computer all day without experiencing any breathing difficulties whatsoever.
ideas: thinks his lungs are out of shape or his airway muscles freeze up when breathing icy air rapidly
concerns: worried he will have to quit playing competitive university football because he cannot catch his breath on the pitch
expectations: wants a quick-acting inhaler that he can use right before football matches to prevent the tightness
social_hx: never smoked, zero alcohol, university sports science student and competitive footballer

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes confirming exercise-induced bronchoconstriction and selecting clinician-directed reliever/pre-exercise therapy with an inhaled corticosteroid-containing strategy when appropriate, adapted to symptom frequency, individual risk factors, and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden chest tightness, wheezing, and coughing while exercising in cold air

Key HPI features: 2-year history of reproducible, predictable episodes of acute shortness of breath, chest tightness, audible wheezing, and dry coughing that occur almost exclusively 5 to 10 minutes after initiating high-intensity aerobic exercise (especially running outdoor football matches or cycling in cold winter air). Symptoms peak 5 to 10 minutes after stopping exercise and resolve spontaneously within 30 to 45 minutes of rest. Denies waking up at night with coughing, denies shortness of breath during rest at home, and denies seasonal hay fever. Can sit in a classroom or work at his computer all day without experiencing any breathing difficulties whatsoever.

Objective/Exam findings: Perform baseline clinical and physiological evaluation during resting asymptomatic period. Chest auscultation: completely normal vesicular breath sounds with zero wheeze or prolonging of expiration. Baseline Spirometry: completely normal resting FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC ratio (>0.80). Objective Exercise Challenge Provocation Testing (gold standard diagnostic test): perform standardized 6-8 minute treadmill exercise challenge breathing cold/dry air -> measure serial spirometry FEV1 at 5, 10, 15, and 30 minutes post-exercise -> positive diagnostic test confirmed by a fall in FEV1 of >= 10% (often 15-20% drop) from baseline within 10 minutes post-exercise, which reverses completely within 15 minutes after administering inhaled salbutamol. Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO): may help assess type-2 airway inflammation but does not by itself confirm or exclude asthma or exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
Relevant background/PMH: none, healthy university athlete
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out exercise-induced bronchoconstriction or asthma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Vocal cord dysfunction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as a silent chest, inability to speak in full sentences, cyanosis, exhaustion, or worsening hypoxaemia.
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis with objective testing and have a clinician select an appropriate inhaled corticosteroid-containing reliever/pre-exercise strategy, inhaler technique education, and a written action plan; avoid relying on SABA alone as ongoing treatment.

If symptoms are frequent, break through despite pre-exercise treatment, or occur outside exercise, reassess adherence/technique and evaluate for underlying asthma and alternative diagnoses before stepping up controller therapy.
Use a progressive warm-up and cold-air humidification/barrier as tolerated, and stop exercise and seek urgent assessment for severe or non-resolving symptoms.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 22M university athlete presents with 2-year history of exercise-induced bronchospasm triggered predictably by cold-air aerobic exertion, with completely normal baseline resting breathing.
reference_soap.objective: Perform baseline clinical and physiological evaluation during resting asymptomatic period. Chest auscultation: completely normal vesicular breath sounds with zero wheeze or prolonging of expiration. Baseline Spirometry: completely normal resting FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC ratio (>0.80). Objective Exercise Challenge Provocation Testing (gold standard diagnostic test): perform standardized 6-8 minute treadmill exercise challenge breathing cold/dry air -> measure serial spirometry FEV1 at 5, 10, 15, and 30 minutes post-exercise -> positive diagnostic test confirmed by a fall in FEV1 of >= 10% (often 15-20% drop) from baseline within 10 minutes post-exercise, which reverses completely within 15 minutes after administering inhaled salbutamol. Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO): may help assess type-2 airway inflammation but does not by itself confirm or exclude asthma or exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
reference_soap.assessment: Suspected exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, pending objective confirmation; assess for coexisting asthma. DDx: Exercise-Induced Laryngeal Obstruction (EILO / Vocal Cord Dysfunction -> causes inspiratory stridor during maximum exertion rather than post-exercise expiratory wheeze, and fails to respond to salbutamol), cardiac arrhythmia, physiological deconditioning.
reference_soap.plan: Arrange objective assessment with spirometry and an appropriately supervised exercise/bronchoprovocation test; evaluate alternatives and coexisting asthma if findings or symptoms are atypical. A clinician should select an inhaled corticosteroid-containing reliever/pre-exercise strategy, teach inhaler technique, and provide an action plan; frequent symptoms, breakthrough symptoms, or symptoms outside exercise require review before controller escalation. Use a progressive warm-up and cold-air humidification/barrier as tolerated. Stop exercise and obtain emergency care for a silent chest, inability to speak in full sentences, cyanosis, severe breathlessness, exhaustion, confusion, or symptoms that do not promptly improve.

learning_objectives: Differentiate Exercise-Induced Bronchospasm (post-exercise expiratory wheeze) from Exercise-Induced Laryngeal Obstruction (peak-exercise inspiratory stridor)
Interpret standardized exercise challenge provocation testing confirming diagnostic >=10% drop in FEV1 post-exertion
Select clinician-directed pre-exercise and reliever therapy while recognising when frequent symptoms require reassessment for controller treatment
Formulate non-pharmacological preventative protocols including structured sprint warm-up refractory induction and cold-air humidification

teaching.one_liner: Chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by variable expiratory airflow limitation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
red_flags: Silent chest, inability to speak in full sentences, cyanosis, or exhaustion
Severe breathlessness at rest, confusion, or worsening hypoxaemia
Symptoms that do not promptly improve after stopping exercise and using the prescribed action plan

must_ask.say: Do you hear a high-pitched whistling sound when you breathe out or feel chest tightness?
Are your coughing and wheezing attacks worse late at night or early in the morning?
Do cold air, exercise, pollen, dust mites, or pet dander trigger your breathlessness?
Do you or your family members have allergic rhinitis, hay fever, or eczema?
How quickly does your blue rescue inhaler open up your chest during an attack?
